blocks.text: The Quiet Machine by Claerbout at the Fondazione MAST is a challenging surprise

The Quiet Machine , the first major solo exhibition in Italy by Belgian artist David Claerbout , is showing at the Fondazione MAST in Bologna. It explores the relationship between industry, technology and nature through a series of images that come together to create an intriguing balance between reality and the unreal.

Curated by Francesco Zanot, this exhibition is one of the most comprehensive retrospectives of Claerbout’s work. Nine film installations, including two previously unseen works, and a dozen drawings are on display on the first floor of MAST, alongside a site-specific installation on the ground floor.

Complexity is a key feature of this exhibition. After all, Claerbout began his career as a painter, then moved towards photography, film, and new media, producing works in which these disciplines exist both individually and in combination with one another.

His works are the result of a sophisticated and constantly updated computational infrastructure: photographs taken in different places and at different times are used as source material and recomposed into a single visual flow; 3D modelling, animation, generative software and artificial intelligence all contribute to creating images that are as realistic as they are unreal, in which reality and fiction intertwine, challenging our perception of time and image. And thus, a well-balanced and sophisticated blend of elements creates a stunning visual impact, with time assuming an essential role.

The author shapes time, fragmenting it or stretching it out. It is closely related to the duration of his works, as they are not created in the blink of an eye: their creation can take a whole day or stretch on indefinitely, as in the case of his real-time computer-generated film. Temporality and duration result in suspended images that suggest a continuous process of changing, whilst excluding events. The focus, therefore, is on the process, turning the works into “quiet machines” amidst the proliferation of images that are continually produced, consumed and forgotten.

Yet again, layered realities emerge, culminating in something imperceptibly unreal. This also applies to another theme explored by David Claerbout: nature, which is conceived as part of a continuum with the technological world. So, according to the author, the forest and the algorithm, plant growth and industrial production all follow the same principle, namely that nothing is static; nothing is ever truly complete. Another theme is work, which is also depicted and enacted in a variety of dimensions. There is the artist’s theoretical and technical work, that of the machine (the software, the algorithm, the graphics engine), that of the film’s protagonists and, certainly not least, that of the visitors.

Finally, the films: nine in total, from 2009 to the present. First is Sunrise , which shows a maid tidying a house still shrouded in darkness before its inhabitants wake up. Once her work is done, she walks away, while night gives way to dawn. Then, Breathing Bird , in which two birds, facing each other, enter each other’s field of vision while remaining physically separated by a pane of glass.

Then, Oil Workers (from the Shell company of Nigeria, returning home from work, caught in torrential rain) . Meticulously constructed using 3D modelling software from a small JPEG image found online, it depicts a group of men taking shelter from the monsoon rain and looking forward to better times, both in terms of the weather and, perhaps, in life.

The Woodcarver and the Forest , a 24-hour film, centres on a man who slowly carves thousands of wooden spoons while the forest around him gradually disappears. Through minimal, repetitive actions, Claerbout establishes a connection between the time for manual labour and that of environmental transformation.

In The Close and Aircraft (F.A.L.) , an aeroplane is depicted floating inside an industrial warehouse, suspended between assembly and abandonment. Claerbout combines the real space with an elaborate digital reconstruction to create the illusion of a photographic reality. The aeroplane seems both to be under construction and already obsolete, superimposing the future and the past in an impossible sense of time.

Finally, Eagle Eye , a previously unseen film lasting several hours. It centres on an eagle lying on an operating table and filmed from various angles. The film, created using archive footage of rescued birds of prey, has been reworked through an animation process combining CGI and generative artificial intelligence, evoking the enigmatic relationship between the artificial and computational realm and organic life.

Another previously unseen work is The Forest and the Wood , which features a digitally constructed larch forest that is gradually felled by a team of virtual workers. The forest is then reconstructed by simply reversing the timeline of the film. Claerbout contrasts the reversibility of the digital world with natural processes.

The exhibition also features twelve drawings that represent another aspect of the artist’s work. Here, technological complexity gives way to the fundamental relationship between thought, manual skill, and the mark. Reflecting on technology is a fundamental part of his artistic practice, contributing to the development of a multifaceted and complex artistic language, though technology never takes centre stage.

A bilingual (Italian and English) booklet published by the MAST Foundation accompanies the exhibition. A series of events for the public, families and children, including talks, presentations and workshops, are free to attend.
David Claerbout : The Quiet Machine 29 October 2026 – 7 February 2027 Fondazione MAST Via Speranza, 42 40133 Bologna www.mast.org
